lessons.title: I am (identity)
lessons.explanation:
Sono + [noun/adjective]
One word opens every self-introduction in Italian.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Sono + [noun/adjective].

items.note: Sono = essere (to be), 1st person singular. No article before a profession: sono medico.

passage.native: I am from Idaho, in the United States.

lessons.title: I have
lessons.objective: I have / I am [age] years old
lessons.explanation:
Ho + [noun]
Avere expresses possession AND age — two essentials in one verb.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Ho + [noun].

items.note: Ho ... anni = I have [X] years. The h is silent: ho sounds like the letter o.

passage.target: Ho uno studio medico a Twin Falls.
passage.native: I have a medical office in Twin Falls.

lessons.title: I like / I love
lessons.objective: I like [thing] / I like to [do something]
lessons.explanation:
Mi piace + [noun / infinitive]
Piacere works backwards — the thing 'pleases you.' Learn it once, describe everything you enjoy.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Mi piace + [noun / infinitive].

items.note: Mi piace + infinitive = I like to... Several things take piacciono: mi piacciono i libri.

passage.native: I like to read in the evening.

lessons.title: I want to
lessons.explanation:
Voglio + [infinitive]
Voglio + any verb = any desire. The most direct way to say what you want.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Voglio + [infinitive].

items.native: I want to speak Italian fluently.
items.note: Voglio + infinitive, nothing in between. The gli in voglio sounds like the lli in million.

passage.native: I want to speak Italian fluently.
I want to help my patients.
I want to learn more words.

lessons.title: I have to
lessons.objective: I have to / I must [do something]
lessons.explanation:
Devo + [infinitive]
This single pattern turns every verb you know into an obligation sentence.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Devo + [infinitive].

items.native: I have to perform surgery at seven.
items.note: Devo + [operare]: any infinitive works, with no che or di in between.

passage.native: I have to perform surgery at seven.

lessons.title: Going to
lessons.explanation:
Present tense + [time word]
Italian has no 'going to' form: the present tense, often with a time word, covers the near future.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Present tense + [time word].

items.native: I'm going to explain the procedure to you now.
items.note: Spiego = I explain / I'm going to explain. Le (capital L) = to you, polite.

passage.native: I'm going to explain the procedure to you now.
We're going to arrive at three.
What are you going to do afterwards?

lessons.title: I can
lessons.objective: I can / I am able to [do something]
lessons.explanation:
Posso + [infinitive]
Potere covers permission and possibility; a learned skill takes sapere: so nuotare.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Posso + [infinitive].

items.native: I can help you with that.
items.note: aiutarti = aiutare + ti: the pronoun attaches to the infinitive, which drops its final e.

passage.native: I can help you with that.
Can you explain it more slowly?

lessons.title: Because
lessons.explanation:
[clause] perché [reason]
Perché links any two ideas with cause and effect, and it also asks 'why?'
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using [clause] perché [reason].

items.target: Studio l'italiano perché voglio comunicare con i miei pazienti.
items.native: I study Italian because I want to communicate with my patients.
items.note: Perché = because AND why. The final é is closed and stressed: per-KAY.

passage.target: Studio l'italiano perché voglio comunicare con i miei pazienti.
passage.native: I study Italian because I want to communicate with my patients.

passage.target: Non posso andare perché devo lavorare.
passage.native: I can't go because I have to work.

passage.target: Sono arrivato in ritardo perché c'era molto traffico.
passage.native: I arrived late because there was a lot of traffic.

lessons.title: I am (condition or place)
lessons.objective: how you are and where you are
lessons.explanation:
Sto + [bene / male] · Sono + [place]
Stare is for how you feel; essere is for where you are and most other conditions.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Sto + [bene / male] · Sono + [place].

items.note: Health takes stare: sto bene, sto male, come sta? Most other states take essere: sono stanco.

passage.native: I am in the waiting room.

lessons.title: Essere or avere
lessons.objective: the same adjective changes meaning with each verb
lessons.explanation:
essere vs avere + [freddo / caldo]
È freddo means he is cold (unfriendly). Ha freddo means he feels cold.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using essere vs avere + [freddo / caldo].

items.native: He is cold toward everyone. (a trait)
items.note: Essere + freddo describes the person or thing; avere + freddo is how the body feels.

passage.native: He is cold toward everyone. (a trait)

passage.target: Il tè è caldo. / Ho caldo.
passage.native: The tea is hot. / I feel hot.

lessons.title: There is / there are
lessons.explanation:
C'è + [singular] · Ci sono + [plural]
Italian changes with number: c'è for one thing, ci sono for more.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using C'è + [singular] · Ci sono + [plural].

items.note: c'è = ci + è, said 'cheh'. The question is the same sentence with a rising voice.

lessons.title: Present tense
lessons.objective: routines and what is happening now
lessons.explanation:
parlo / prendi / dorme
The ending carries the subject, so you can drop the pronoun.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using parlo / prendi / dorme.

items.note: The -o ending already means 'I': io is optional.

lessons.title: Negation
lessons.explanation:
non + [verb]
One word before the verb, and double negatives are correct here.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using non + [verb].

items.note: Non goes right before the verb: non capisco. Capire adds -isc-: capisco, capisci, capisce.

lessons.title: Question words
lessons.explanation:
Dove / Quando / Quanto / Perché…?
No special punctuation or word order: a rising voice turns a statement into a question.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Dove / Quando / Quanto / Perché…?.

items.note: dove + è = dov'è: the vowels merge under an apostrophe.

lessons.title: I would like
lessons.explanation:
Vorrei / Mi piacerebbe + [infinitive]
Voglio is fine with friends; vorrei is what you use at a counter.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Vorrei / Mi piacerebbe + [infinitive].

items.native: I would like a coffee, please.
items.note: Vorrei = conditional of volere. Hold the double r: vor-REI.

passage.native: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like to book a table.
I would like to move the appointment.

lessons.title: I should / I must
lessons.explanation:
Dovrei + [infinitive]
Devo is practical necessity; dovrei is closer to 'ought to'.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Dovrei + [infinitive].

items.note: Dovrei = conditional of dovere: softer than devo, like English 'should'.

lessons.title: I need
lessons.explanation:
Ho bisogno di + [noun/infinitive]
Literally 'I have need of': stronger than voglio, and understood everywhere.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Ho bisogno di + [noun/infinitive].

items.note: bisogno: gn sounds like the ny in canyon.

passage.target: Ho bisogno di vedere un medico.
passage.native: I need to see a doctor.

lessons.title: Reflexive verbs
lessons.explanation:
mi / ti / si + [verb]
Your own name arrives through one: mi chiamo.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using mi / ti / si + [verb].

items.note: Literally 'I call myself Anna'. Ch before i sounds like k: KYAH-mo.

lessons.title: Passato prossimo (completed past)
lessons.objective: a finished action at a finished time
lessons.explanation:
ho parlato / sono andato
What happened and is over: avere or essere + past participle. Verbs of motion take essere.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using ho parlato / sono andato.

items.native: Yesterday I went to the hospital.
items.note: Andare takes essere, and the participle agrees: sono andato (m.), sono andata (f.).

passage.native: Yesterday I went to the hospital.

lessons.title: Imperfetto (ongoing past)
lessons.objective: how things used to be, and background
lessons.explanation:
parlavo / mangiavi / viveva
The passato prossimo is the event; the imperfetto is the scenery around it.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using parlavo / mangiavi / viveva.

items.target: Quando ero bambino, vivevo in campagna.
items.native: When I was a child, I lived in the countryside.
items.note: Ero is the irregular imperfetto of essere: ero, eri, era.

passage.target: Quando ero bambino, vivevo in campagna.
passage.native: When I was a child, I lived in the countryside.
I was studying when you called.

lessons.title: Already, just, not yet
lessons.objective: recent past still connected to now
lessons.explanation:
ho appena / hai già / non ho ancora + [participle]
Italian uses the passato prossimo for recent events too; appena, già and ancora tie them to now.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using ho appena / hai già / non ho ancora + [participle].

items.note: Appena sits between the two parts: ho appena finito.

passage.target: Non sono ancora riuscito a dormire.
passage.native: I still haven't managed to sleep.

lessons.title: Future
lessons.explanation:
parlerò / prenderai / partirà
The present covers most plans; the futuro adds weight or a guess.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using parlerò / prenderai / partirà.

items.note: Uscirò: sc before i sounds like sh, and the stress falls on the final ò.

lessons.title: More than / less than
lessons.explanation:
più / meno + [adjective] + di
One frame for most comparisons; di joins the article that follows (dell', del).

items.target: Questo è più caro di quello.
items.native: This one is more expensive than that one.
items.note: Di = than before a noun or pronoun; che goes between two adjectives or two verbs.

passage.native: This one is more expensive than that one.

lessons.title: The most / very
lessons.objective: the top of a group, or a strong degree
lessons.explanation:
il più + [adjective] · [adjective] + -issimo
-issimo is the ending that adds feeling without adding words.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using il più + [adjective] · [adjective] + -issimo.

items.target: È il miglior ristorante della città.

lessons.title: Object pronouns
lessons.explanation:
lo / la / li / le · mi / ti / gli
They sit before the verb, or attach to the end of an infinitive.

items.note: Lo = it for a masculine thing; la for a feminine one: la prendo.

lessons.title: Per or da

per vs da
Per points forward to a goal or destination; da + present counts time that is still going on.

lessons.title: Subjunctive after wishes

items.native: I have lived in Twin Falls for ten years.
items.note: da + present = still going on: abito qui da dieci anni, I have lived here for ten years (and still do).

passage.target: Studio l'italiano per parlare con i miei pazienti.
passage.native: I study Italian in order to speak with my patients.

passage.target: Abito a Twin Falls da dieci anni.
passage.native: I have lived in Twin Falls for ten years.

lessons.title: Subjunctive after wishes · 2
lessons.objective: wishes, doubts, and requests about someone else
lessons.explanation:
Spero che / Voglio che + [congiuntivo]
Two subjects and a wish between them pull the second verb into the congiuntivo. Credo che and penso che take it too.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Spero che / Voglio che + [congiuntivo].

items.note: Keep tu: in the present congiuntivo io, tu and lui/lei share one form (riposi), so the pronoun shows who.

passage.native: I hope you get better soon.
I do not think it is serious.

lessons.title: I am (identity) · 3
lessons.explanation:
Sono + [noun/adjective]
One word opens every self-introduction in Italian.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Sono + [noun/adjective].

items.note: uno, not un, before s + consonant: uno studente, uno studio.

passage.native: I am from Idaho, in the United States.

lessons.title: I have · 3
lessons.objective: I have / I am [age] years old
lessons.explanation:
Ho + [noun]
Avere expresses possession AND age — two essentials in one verb.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Ho + [noun].

items.target: Ho uno studio medico a Twin Falls.
items.native: I have a medical office in Twin Falls.
items.note: a + city (a Twin Falls, a Roma); in + country or region (in Italia).

passage.target: Ho uno studio medico a Twin Falls.
passage.native: I have a medical office in Twin Falls.

lessons.title: I like / I love · 3
lessons.objective: I like [thing] / I like to [do something]
lessons.explanation:
Mi piace + [noun / infinitive]
Piacere works backwards — the thing 'pleases you.' Learn it once, describe everything you enjoy.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Mi piace + [noun / infinitive].

items.native: I like to read in the evening.
items.note: La sera = in the evening, la mattina = in the morning: no preposition needed.

passage.native: I like to read in the evening.

lessons.title: I want to · 3
lessons.explanation:
Voglio + [infinitive]
Voglio + any verb = any desire. The most direct way to say what you want.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Voglio + [infinitive].

items.native: I want to learn more words.
items.note: Voglio is direct. To a stranger or at a counter, say vorrei (lesson 15).

passage.native: I want to speak Italian fluently.
I want to help my patients.
I want to learn more words.

lessons.title: I have to · 3
lessons.objective: I have to / I must [do something]
lessons.explanation:
Devo + [infinitive]
This single pattern turns every verb you know into an obligation sentence.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Devo + [infinitive].

items.note: Dovere in the present: devo, devi, deve, dobbiamo, dovete, devono.

passage.native: I have to perform surgery at seven.

lessons.title: Going to · 3
lessons.explanation:
Present tense + [time word]
Italian has no 'going to' form: the present tense, often with a time word, covers the near future.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Say the example from memory. Then make your own sentence using Present tense + [time word].

items.native: What are you going to do afterwards?
items.note: Vado a fare means 'I go (somewhere) to do' and needs real movement. For plans, use the present: cosa fai dopo?

passage.native: I'm going to explain the procedure to you now.
We're going to arrive at three.
What are you going to do afterwards?
